# Pronouncing Meru: a guide for the curious

Saying **Meru** aloud is harder than reading it on ​a screen, and more rewarding. The restored spelling is a compressed pronunciation guide: every accent and macron is an instruction. This post unpacks those instructions — the reconstructed sound, the phoneme-by-phoneme record, ‌the kindred forms in neighboring languages — and then zooms out to the full record around the name: its Devanagari writing, its mythology, its cult, and its modern life as a Unicode ‌domain. Whether you arrive as a linguist, a reader of myth, or a domainer, you will leave able to say the name the way the evidence suggests it was said — and ​able to type it the way it was written.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Meru
- **ASCII form:** meru
- **Meaning:** "Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which ​the sun, moon and planets revolve; the Olympus of Hindu mythology and abode of the gods."
- **Domain of influence:** Cosmic Mountain, Axis Mundi
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** मेरु (Devanagari)

## ​Overview

**Meru** (*meru*) — The Axis Mountain, Olympus of the Hindus · Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which the sun, moon and planets revolve — belongs ​to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Cosmic Mountain, Axis Mundi". The name means "Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which the ​sun, moon and planets revolve; the Olympus of Hindu mythology and abode of the gods.".

**Meru** is the world’s axle: the golden mountain at the centre of the cosmos, around which the ‌sun, moon, and planets revolve, on whose summit Indra’s city stands, and whose four faces of gold, crystal, ruby, and lapis feed the four great rivers of the directions. Every Indian cosmology ​— Hindu, Buddhist, Jain — puts Meru in the middle; every mandala is its plan.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Meru** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/meru/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form ​— a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *meru* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form ‌the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **मेरु**. Etymologically it means "Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which ​the sun, moon and planets revolve; the Olympus of Hindu mythology and abode of the gods.".

The ASCII form *meru* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it ‌is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Meru** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. ## ‌The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **मेरु**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Meru*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Meru is written in Devanagari as मेरु
- IAST transliteration ​maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the ​name is **/ˈmɛruː/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Meru).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Me-** — Short e as in “set”; the name is pre-Vedic in feel, its etymology uncertain.
- **-ru** — Long ū as in ​“rule”; the name closes on the resonant liquid.
- **** — The axis mountain — the Olympus of Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology alike.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “MEH-roo”

​Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Buddhist** — Sumeru — “excellent Meru”, the abode of the thirty-three gods
- **Jain** — Meru as the central peak of the middle world

All three ​Indian religions share Meru — the one mountain in the centre of every map.

## Mythology

Meru’s mythology is cosmography — the mountain’s biography is the world’s architecture. It rises from the centre ‌of Jambudvīpa, the rose-apple continent; the sun’s chariot circles it daily; the Ganges falls first on its summit and only then to the earth; and the gods’ wars are fought on its terraces. ​The Purāṇic geographies measure all distance from its base.

### The Mountain of Measure (Purāṇic Cosmography)

The Purāṇas give Meru its statistics: 84,000 leagues high, its base 32,000 across, its summit the square ‌of the gods’ city. The sun’s horses, tired from circling it, rest at night on its western face; the moon’s waxing is the gods’ drinking of the lunar soma on its terraces. ​The mountain is the cosmos’s clock, scale, and sceptre.

### The River’s First Fall (Gangā Cycle)

When Bhagīratha won the Ganges’ descent for his burned ancestors, the river fell first from heaven onto ‌the matted hair of Śiva — and before that, the tradition adds, upon Meru’s summit, where the gods’ gardens divided her into the seven streams. Meru is the river’s first landing, heaven’s ​customs-house.

### The Mountain Diagrammed (Mandala Theology)

The Buddhist and Hindu maṇḍala is Meru flattened into a map: the square’s four gates are its faces, the inner palace the summit’s city, the concentric ‌rings its seven world-encircling ranges. To construct a mandala is to rebuild Meru; to enter it is to climb. The Vajrayāna made the diagram the path itself.

### The Churning’s Spindle (Samudra Manthana)

When ​the gods and demons churned the ocean of milk, the churning-rod was Mandara, Meru’s little brother of a mountain; the serpent Vāsuki the rope. Meru’s family thus supplied the axis of the ‌gods’ greatest work — the axis-mountain’s line, lending itself to every cosmic rotation.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Meru concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed ​statement about the name:

- **The Axis** — The world turns on Meru; the pole star wheels above its summit as the heavens’ nail-head.
- **The Four Faces** — Gold to the east, crystal ​south, ruby west, lapis north — the four colours of the mandala.
- **City of the Gods** — Indra’s Amarāvatī crowns the summit; the thirty-three gods feast in its halls.
- **The Mandala’s Map** ‌— Every maṇḍala diagrams Meru: centre, four gates, and the enclosing world-rings.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Meru survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus ‌is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Meru’s monuments are every stupa and pagoda — the Borobudur terraces walk the pilgrim up Sumeru; the ‌temple mountains of Angkor are Meru in sandstone. The maṇḍala-paintings of Tibet diagram it ten thousand times.

## Across Cultures

Meru is shared property: Hindu Meru, Buddhist ​Sumeru, Jain Meru of the madhyaloka. The Greeks of Bactria heard Olympus in it; and the East Asian Buddhist cosmologies drew Sumeru as the world’s spike on temple banners from Java to ‌Japan. The mountain out-religioned every religion that mapped it.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

Every mandala, stupa, ​and temple plan is a Meru; the prayer-wheel’s axis and the pagoda’s spire are its hardware. ‘Sumeru’ and ‘Meru’ entered the names of a thousand monasteries and mountains — and travellers to ​the real Himalaya argued for centuries which peak the geographers had meant.

## A Meditation

Meru: the name of the centre, restored at the centre of a plain line of letters. It needs no diacritic — the mountain carries its own ‌height, and every reader’s eye climbs it. Two syllables, eighty-four thousand leagues.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case ​of **Meru**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *meru* and ​the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries ​semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized ‌differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **m**, **e**, **r**, **u** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. ​What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

Its sphere — Cosmic Mountain, Axis Mundi — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. ​The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Meru**, it marks ‌the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes ‌the status of the restoration. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is ‌the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For ‌**Meru**, the chain begins with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "Name of a ​fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which the sun, moon and planets revolve; the Olympus of Hindu mythology and abode of the gods." anchors the name in its semantic ​field; without that anchor, the marks would float free of the figure they name. The restored form **Meru** and the ASCII form *meru* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a ​conventional capitalization rather than a recovery of lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Meru aSCII-equivalent form. The ​rule is mechanical, not editorial, which means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced ‌it, because every step is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
